levels.def: The part of the computer that does the actual work. It reads one tiny instruction at a time and does exactly that, billions of times a second.
The processor. It runs one instruction stream per core. JavaScript in a browser gets one main stream, which is why long loops freeze the page.
The computer's short-term desk. Fast, small, wiped when the power goes. Programs and the values they are working on live here while running.
Numbered slots. A variable is a name for a slot. Two names can point at the same slot, which is why changing one object can change 'another'.
A named chunk of saved stuff on the disk. Code is files. Photos are files. Your saved Memento data is a file-like thing the browser keeps.
Bytes on disk with a name and a path. On iOS and in databases, 'file' is a looser idea: data is stored in containers you do not see as files.
A list of instructions the CPU can follow. Written by a human (or an AI), saved as a file, run by the computer.
From the shell's side: a file somewhere on the PATH that can be run by name. A script you write is a program in exactly the same sense.
A program that is currently running. Memento in Safari is one process. The server answering it is another, on a different computer.
A running program with its own memory and an id number (PID). The terminal can list them and kill them.
Instructions written in a language a human can read and a computer can be made to follow.
The language that runs inside web browsers. Memento's web app is written in it.
A language with values, variables, functions and objects. Runs in browsers, in Node on servers, and inside React Native on phones.
Everything the app currently remembers. In Memento it is one big object called state.
The single source of truth the screen is drawn from. Events change state; the screen is updated from state, never edited on its own.
A computer somewhere else that answers requests. You never see it. Memento's servers are rented from Supabase.
A program that listens on an address and runs a function for each request. 'Serverless' still means a server, just one somebody else keeps warm.
Where saved data lives on the server side, organised so it can be found again.
Tables of rows with keys that relate them, guarded by rules (like Row Level Security) that decide who may see which rows.
An agreed way for two programs to talk to each other.
A contract: these addresses, these verbs, this JSON in, this JSON out, these status codes.
Memento's API is a handful of Supabase edge functions and one Postgres function. The phone never talks to Anthropic or Polar directly.
The wires and radio between your phone and the server. Slow compared to memory, and it can fail.
A small storage box the browser gives each website. Memento's web app saves your whole state there under one key.
A key-value store, strings only, about 5 MB, per website origin. Can throw when full or in private mode, so every write is wrapped in try/catch.
The part of the app you can see and touch. Runs on your device.
The part that runs on servers you never see: accounts, the database, the AI calls.
The company Memento rents its backend from: accounts, a database, and small server functions.
Founded January 2020 as the open-source answer to Firebase, built on Postgres. It is the newest floor under Memento, and the youngest thing in the whole stack.
A middleman. Memento's phone never calls the AI directly; it calls Memento's own small server, which calls the AI with a secret key the phone never sees.
A text window where you type commands to the computer instead of clicking. Nothing magic: each line is a program's name plus what to give it.
A shell (zsh on your Mac) reading lines, finding the program named first via PATH, running it with the rest as arguments, and printing what it says.
The address of a file: the folders you walk through to reach it, joined with slashes.
The tool that records every change to a codebase, so nothing is ever lost and two people can work on the same files.
A history of snapshots (commits), each pointing at the one before, stored in the hidden .git folder.
A graph of snapshots. Branches are movable labels on it. A merge joins two lines of history.
A saved snapshot of the whole folder, with a message and an id (the hash).
A label that points at a commit and moves forward as you add commits. Not a copy of the folder.
Joining two lines of history into one. A conflict is two edits to the same line, which a human resolves.
A request on GitHub to merge one branch into another, with a page where people review the changes first.
A name tag on a value. Not a box: the value does not live inside the name.
A name bound to a value. For objects, the value is a reference, so two names can point at one object.
A named recipe. Define it once, call it whenever. It takes inputs (parameters) and can hand back a result (return).
The pile of functions currently running. Call one, it goes on top. It returns, it comes off. A stack trace is a photo of this pile.
A bundle of named values. { name: 'Malik', streak: 4 }.
Work that finishes later. await means 'come back to this line when the answer arrives', and the app keeps responding meanwhile.
The JavaScript command that sends a request over the network and gives you a promise of the reply.
The live tree of elements the browser builds from your HTML. JavaScript changes the page by changing this tree.
The rules for a request and a reply on the web: an address, a verb (GET, POST), headers, a body, and a status code back.
Text that looks like a JavaScript object. The envelope most APIs use to send data.
A string that proves who you are for a while, sent with each request. Expires, can be refreshed, can be revoked.
A named value the operating system hands to a program when it starts. How secrets get in without being written in the code.
Someone else's code your app needs. Listed in package.json with a version, downloaded by npm.
Copying a version of the app to the place users reach it. In Memento, a robot does it on every push to main.
JavaScript with a proofreader. You describe shapes (types); the compiler checks them before anything runs.
A way to write iPhone and Android apps in JavaScript/TypeScript. It draws real native views, not a web page.
A photograph of the call stack at the moment something broke: the function that failed, then who called it, then who called that.
The list of function calls that were in progress when an error happened. Read it top down: the top line is where it broke.
Code that runs your code and checks the answer. A failing test is a spec for what should be true.
A database rule deciding which rows each signed-in user may see or change. Missing it is what exposed 170 Lovable apps and Moltbook, both on the same backend Memento uses.
A database rule that says which rows each signed-in user may see or change. Without it, a public key reads everyone's data.
When an AI states something that is not true with full confidence: a file that does not exist, a function that was never written, 'tests pass' with no output.
Accepting whatever the AI produces without reading it. Fine for a toy. Fatal for a product with users.
A hard job done once and wrapped in a name, so nobody has to do it again. Every layer under your app is one of these, stacked.
The numbers a CPU actually eats. Specific to one kind of chip. Written by hand in the 1950s, produced by tools ever since.
A program that turns human-readable code into machine instructions. Fortran, 1957. The first great abstraction, and the shape of every layer after it.
Code published for anyone to read, use and change. The reason nobody starts from zero, and the reason Memento can rent a backend built in public.
Renting somebody else's computers by the hour instead of buying your own. Started in 2006. Without it a solo founder cannot host anything.
One command that downloads other people's code into your project, each piece with a version number. npm shipped in January 2010.
Borrowed code with opinions. A library you call; a framework calls you. React, from 2013, is the one Memento's rebuild uses.
A tool that reads all your source files, works out the order, and produces one file the browser loads. Memento's web app deliberately has none.
The language for asking a database questions and changing what it stores. Memento has 33 SQL migration files.
A model given tools, a terminal, and permission to act in a loop until a job is done. What changed from 2025 onward is how long it can run unattended, not how clever a single answer is.
A standard test a model is scored on, like SWE-bench Verified. Useful, gameable, self-reported by the vendor, and it saturates once everyone scores in the nineties.
The scaffolding around an agent: rule files it reads every session, plan files, checks and hooks. Memento's CLAUDE.md and MIGRATION folder are one.
The exact list of lines a change added and removed. The thing you read before approving anything. Chapter 7 teaches you to read one.
The difference between two versions of a file, shown as removed and added lines. git diff compares the working folder to the staging area; git diff --staged compares staging to the last snapshot.
How much text a model can hold at once. Opus 4.8 and Opus 5 hold about a million tokens. It still ends, and when it does, anything not written to a file is gone.
A named container of files and other folders. Engineers usually say directory. The whole machine is one nest of them starting at /.
A path starting at / or ~. It means the same thing typed from anywhere on the machine.
A path starting with a name, measured from the folder you are standing in. js/01-state-foundation.js only means something if you are in memento-app.
Your own top-level folder, /Users/<name> on a Mac. The shell writes it as ~ and swaps the real path in before a command runs.
The folder the Terminal is standing in right now. pwd prints it, cd changes it, and every relative path is measured from it.
A file whose name starts with a dot, like .git or .gitignore. Not secret, just not listed by default. Often the tooling that matters most.
A program for reading and writing a whole folder of code: file tree, project-wide search, go to definition, find references, clickable path:line links. VS Code and Cursor are the common ones.
The program reading your typed lines. On a Mac it is zsh. It reads a line, finds the program you named, runs it with the rest as arguments, and prints what came back.
A program plus what you hand it. One grammar, every time: name first, then arguments.
Anything after the program's name on the line. Usually what to work on.
The actual value you hand over when calling a function, which gets tied to the parameter name.
An argument starting with a dash, like -n or --help. The dials on a program. Ask any program for its list with --help.
The ordered list of folders the shell searches for a program name. 'command not found' means the name was not in any of them. which node shows which file a name resolved to.
The channel a program prints its answer on. This is the one a pipe or a > redirect captures.
The second channel, for complaints. It lands in the same window but travels separately, which is why errors still appear after you redirect the output. Silence it with 2>/dev/null.
The number a program leaves behind when it finishes. 0 means it worked, anything else means it did not. echo $? shows the last one. This is what CI and && read.
The | character. Feeds one program's stdout straight into the next program's input, so small tools combine into big ones.
The > character. Writes stdout into a file instead of the screen, overwriting whatever was there with no prompt and no undo. >> appends instead.
A project folder plus its hidden .git folder, which holds every snapshot ever taken of it.
The real files on disk that you and the agents edit. Nothing here is in a snapshot until you add and commit it.
The waiting room. It holds the exact file versions that will go into the next snapshot. git add <file> puts one in.
A commit's id: a fingerprint calculated from the snapshot's contents and its parent's id. Same contents, same fingerprint. Change anything and every id after it changes too.
The commit a commit points back at. Following parents backwards walks the whole history of the project.
A merge commit has two parents, which is why history is a graph rather than a straight line.
Git's word for the snapshot you are currently standing on.

A label meaning 'where you are'. It points at a branch label, which is how git knows which one to move forward when you commit. Switching branches moves HEAD and rewrites your working folder to match.
Two lines of work changed the same lines of one file, differently. Git stops, writes both versions into the file with markers, and waits for a human to pick. Not a breakage.

Replaying your commits on top of someone else's latest work instead of joining with a merge commit. Gives one straight line and brand new hashes, so it is for your own unpushed work. Memento's standing instruction is git pull --rebase.
Another copy of the repository, usually on a server. push sends commits to it, pull fetches its commits and combines them with yours.
The conventional name for a project's main remote. Memento's origin is the private GitHub repo malikpeace/memento.
A new commit that undoes an earlier one. History grows and nothing is lost, so it is safe on work other people already have. What 'roll back the deploy' means.

Moving your branch label backwards. git reset --hard also overwrites your working folder, destroying uncommitted work with no undo, and rewrites what others build on if the commits were pushed. Banned in Memento.
A private local log of every position HEAD has been in, including ones no label points at any more. How you find a lost commit's hash. Never pushed, and entries expire after about 30 to 90 days.
A piece of data sitting in memory: the number 7, the text 'stellar', true. It exists whether or not anything has named it.
What kind of thing a value is. The machine picks which rule to apply from the type, which is why '7' and 7 behave completely differently.
Text. The quotes are what make it text. Everything a user types and everything read from storage starts as one.
A number, written with no quotes. Whole numbers and decimals are the same type in JavaScript.
true or false. Only those two values exist. Memento's isPaid is one.
Deliberately empty. A human wrote it to say 'there is nothing here on purpose', like paidAt before anyone has paid.
Never given a value. Nobody decided anything. Different from null, which somebody chose.
Also what a function hands back when it has no return. The usual reason a call 'works' but prints nothing useful.
An ordered list, written in square brackets. Memento's clarity.answers.domains starts as an empty one.
A name that may never be pointed at something else. It locks the name, not the object behind it: const state = {...} still allows state.streak = 5.
Asks a value what type it is. The cheapest debugging tool in the language and the first move when a value behaves strangely.
Same type and same value. Always use it. The two-equals version converts types first, so it claims '7' == 7 is true.
Text in backticks with ${...} holes that values get dropped into. Most of Memento's screen copy and AI prompts are built this way.
A line starting with // that the machine skips entirely. Humans talking to humans across time.
A named blank in a function definition. It is a name tag that exists only while the function is running.
Hands a value back to whoever called, and stops the function immediately. Lines below a return that ran are dead.
A check at the top of a function that returns early on a bad case, so the real work below stays flat. Memento's persistState() and sendAiAnswer() both open with one.
A shorter spelling of a function: (a, b) => a + b. Same idea, used most when a function is being handed to something else to call later.
Where a name is visible. Names made inside a function live on that function's stack card and are thrown away when it returns.
